entries.definition: A business owned by one person. Simplest to set up, keeps all the profit and all the decisions, but carries **unlimited liability**.
entries.example: A plumber trading in their own name. If the business cannot pay a supplier, the supplier can pursue the owner's own car and savings.

entries.definition: A business owned by two or more people who share the capital, the work, the decisions and the profit. In an ordinary partnership every partner still has **unlimited liability** for the whole debt.
entries.example: Three accountants in partnership: each is liable for all the firm's debts, including one run up by another partner, which is why partners must trust each other.

entries.definition: An **incorporated** business, registered at Companies House as a separate legal person from its owners. The owners are shareholders with **limited liability**, and it can sell shares privately.
entries.example: Two friends needing £60 000 for a bakery form an Ltd: they can sell shares to family, and if it fails they lose only what they invested.

entries.definition: The owner and the business are the same in law, so there is no limit to what the owner can lose. Personal possessions can be taken to pay business debts.
entries.example: A sole trader's cancelled order leaves them owing a supplier: the supplier can pursue the owner personally, not just the business.

entries.definition: The company is a separate legal person, so its debts are its own. A shareholder can only lose the money they paid for their shares.
entries.example: A shareholder who put £5000 into an Ltd that fails owing £80 000 loses the £5000 and no more; their home is safe.

entries.definition: Paying a **franchisor** for the right to trade using their brand, products and proven system. It is a way of starting, not a legal structure, and sits on top of whichever structure is chosen.
entries.example: A sandwich-shop franchisee pays a £15 000 fee and 8% of revenue, and in return gets a name customers know, training and supplies.

entries.definition: The ongoing payment a franchisee makes to the franchisor, usually a percentage of revenue. It leaves the business on every sale, for as long as the franchise lasts.
entries.example: At 8% of revenue, a franchise taking £200 000 a year pays £16 000, so it keeps less profit than an independent shop with the same sales.

entries.definition: The four decisions a business makes to sell to its target market: **product, price, promotion and place**. They must be consistent with each other and with the customer.
entries.example: A luxury handbag at a high price, sold in a discount supermarket with buy-one-get-one-free offers, sends four different messages and customers trust none of them.

entries.definition: Selling online through a website or app. It changes **place** in the marketing mix, lets a business reach the whole country from a low-cost location, and cuts the need for expensive premises.
entries.example: A jewellery maker selling from a website has no rent and a national market; a hairdresser cannot, because the customer has to be there.

entries.definition: A document setting out the idea, the aims and objectives, the target market, the forecast revenue, costs and cash flow, the finance and the marketing mix.
entries.example: A bakery's plan forecasts 500 loaves a week at £3, £6000 of fixed costs and a £10 000 loan; the bank reads the cash-flow page first.

entries.definition: Anyone with an interest in what a business does. **Internal**: owners, employees, managers. **External**: customers, suppliers, the local community, pressure groups and the government.
entries.example: A supermarket opening 24 hours pleases owners (more profit) and annoys residents (lorries at 3 a.m.) — the conflict is what a 9-mark question is really asking about.

entries.definition: An organisation campaigning on a single issue that can influence a business through publicity, boycotts and pressure on politicians.
entries.example: A group campaigning against a factory's pollution generates bad publicity, so customers stay away and the business may have to change its methods.

entries.definition: The four kinds on the specification: e-commerce, social media, digital communication and payment systems. Each changes sales, costs and the marketing mix, and is a threat to a business that ignores it.
entries.example: A bookshop adding click-and-collect and an Instagram account changes place and promotion for almost no cost; one that ignores both loses customers to a rival that does not.

entries.definition: The law protecting customers: goods must be of **satisfactory quality**, **fit for purpose** and **as described**, and adverts must not mislead.
entries.example: A kettle that fails after a week is not of satisfactory quality, so the customer is entitled to a refund, repair or replacement.

entries.definition: The law protecting workers: no discrimination in recruitment or at work, at least the minimum wage, and a safe workplace with training and equipment.
entries.example: A furniture maker taking on three staff must pay the minimum wage, give paid holiday and guard the machinery, or face fines and compensation claims.

entries.definition: Laws a business must obey. Meeting them costs money; breaking them usually costs more, in fines, compensation, closure and lost trust.
entries.example: Complying with health and safety means buying guards and protective equipment; not complying can mean a fine, a claim from an injured worker, or being closed down.

entries.definition: The state of the economy as a whole, which a business cannot control: unemployment, consumer income, inflation, interest rates, taxation and exchange rates.
entries.example: A café near a factory that is closing faces rising local unemployment and falling sales, while a rise in interest rates raises its loan repayments at the same time.

entries.definition: A general rise in prices over time. It raises a business's costs and reduces what customers' incomes can buy.
entries.example: Inflation raises a bakery's flour costs, so its cost per loaf rises, so unless it raises prices its profit per loaf falls. That chain is what a 6-mark answer needs.

entries.definition: The cost of borrowing money. Higher rates make a business's loans dearer **and** leave customers with mortgages less to spend, so it is hit twice.
entries.example: A café with a loan sees its repayments rise while its customers, paying more on their mortgages, spend less. Both effects squeeze profit.

entries.definition: How much foreign currency one pound buys. To turn foreign currency into pounds, **divide** by the rate. Remember **SPICED**: Strong Pound, Imports Cheaper, Exports Dearer.
entries.example: At £1 = €1.25 a €40 pair of jeans costs £32; if the pound weakens to £1 = €1.10 the same jeans cost £36.36, so the importer's costs rise by £4.36.

entries.definition: An **aim** is what the business wants overall; an **objective** is a measurable target on the way. Financial objectives are survival, profit, sales, market share and security; non-financial ones include independence, personal satisfaction, challenge and social aims.
entries.example: *Be the best-known bakery in town* is an aim; *sell 500 loaves a week by December* is an objective. A start-up's first objective is usually survival.

entries.definition: The money coming in from sales: price × quantity sold. It is **not** profit, because no costs have been taken off.
entries.example: 200 coffees at £3 gives revenue of £600. If the costs were £450, the profit is £150 — the revenue is still £600.

entries.definition: Costs that do not change with output: rent, salaries, insurance, loan repayments. They are paid whether the business sells anything or not.
entries.example: A café paying £1200 a month rent pays it whether it sells 100 coffees or 1000. That £1200 is what goes on the top of the break-even formula.

entries.definition: Costs that rise with every unit made or sold: materials, ingredients, packaging. Total costs are fixed plus variable.
entries.example: Ingredients at £0.90 a loaf: 800 loaves cost £720 in variable costs, and with £1200 of fixed costs the total is £1920.

entries.definition: What is left when total costs are taken from revenue. A negative figure is a **loss**.
entries.example: Revenue £8000, fixed costs £2500, variable costs £3000: total costs £5500, so profit is £2500.

entries.definition: The output at which revenue exactly covers total costs: no profit, no loss. Break-even output = fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost per unit).
entries.example: Fixed costs £6000, price £25, variable cost £10: each sale contributes £15, so break-even is $\dfrac{6000}{15} = 400$ units.

entries.definition: What each sale puts towards the fixed costs: price minus variable cost per unit. It is the bottom of the break-even formula.
entries.example: Selling at £25 with a £10 variable cost gives a contribution of £15. Raising the price to £30 raises it to £20, so break-even falls from 400 units to 300.

entries.definition: How far actual sales are above break-even: the fall in sales the business could survive before making a loss.
entries.example: Break-even 400 units, actual sales 650: the margin of safety is 250 units. If rent rises and break-even goes to 500, the margin shrinks to 150.

entries.definition: The money actually moving in and out of the bank, and **when**. Different from profit, which is a total for the year. A profitable business can still run out of cash.
entries.example: A furniture maker pays for timber in March but is not paid for the finished order until May, so the cash goes out before it comes in.

entries.definition: A month-by-month prediction of money in and out, so a shortage can be seen coming. Net cash flow = inflows − outflows; closing balance = opening balance + net cash flow, and each closing balance becomes the next opening balance.
entries.example: Opening £2000, January net +£500 gives a closing balance of £2500; February net −£3200 takes it to −£700, so an overdraft is needed that month.

entries.definition: Short-term finance letting a bank account go below zero up to an agreed limit. Flexible, but the interest is charged daily and the rate is high.
entries.example: A business facing a −£700 closing balance in February arranges an overdraft to cover it, then repays it in March when the cash comes back in.

entries.definition: Long-term finance: a fixed sum repaid with interest over years. The owner keeps full ownership, but the repayments are due whether or not the business does well.
entries.example: Borrow £10 000 and repay £11 500: the interest is £1500, which is $\dfrac{1500}{10\,000} \times 100 = 15\%$ of the amount borrowed.

entries.definition: Money raised by selling shares in a company. There is nothing to repay, but the new shareholders own part of the business and a share of its profit for ever.
entries.example: An investor offering £50 000 for 40% of a café takes 40% of the profit of every branch, for as long as the business exists — usually dearer than a loan for a proven business.

entries.definition: The structure that earns marks in Business: start from a fact in the case, then *this means… which leads to…*, ending in an effect on the business's sales, costs, profit or reputation.
entries.example: *Inflation raises the bakery's flour costs, so its cost per loaf rises, so unless it raises prices its profit per loaf falls.* An answer true of any business is capped at the bottom level.

entries.definition: The 9-mark command word: choose one option, give developed reasons for it **and** against the other, both applied to the case, then a judgement that names the deciding factor.
entries.example: Choosing a bank loan over an investor: reasons for, reasons against the investor, then *the deciding factor is that the café is proven, so it can service a loan and keep its ownership*.

entries.definition: The 12-mark command word: developed chains on both sides, applied throughout, then a judgement using *it depends on*, naming the condition and saying how the answer would change if it were different.
entries.example: On whether technology helps a bookshop: *it depends on whether the shop uses the technology or only suffers it* — a shop competing on price loses, one competing on service gains.

entries.definition: The particular group of customers a business aims its product at. Every part of the marketing mix has to fit that group; a mix that suits nobody in particular suits nobody at all.
entries.example: A premium skincare range aimed at buyers who value quality: a high price, glossy magazine adverts and department-store samples all agree. Half-price offers in a discount store would contradict them.

entries.definition: A person who spots a business opportunity, organises the resources to pursue it, makes the business decisions, and takes the risk that it may fail, in return for the possible reward.
entries.example: Someone who leaves a salaried job to open a bakery is risking their savings and income for the chance of profit and independence.

entries.definition: The risks of starting a business are business failure, financial loss and lack of security. The rewards are business success, profit and independence. Entrepreneurs accept the risks for the chance of the rewards.
entries.example: A start-up that fails can lose the founder's savings; one that succeeds can pay them more than a job ever did.

entries.definition: The difference between the price a business sells for and the cost of the materials that went into it. It is created by convenience, branding, quality, design and unique selling points — not the same as profit, which also takes running costs off.
entries.example: A coffee shop pays pence for beans and milk but sells the cup for £3: the difference is added value.

entries.definition: Collecting information about customers, the market and competitors to identify and understand customer needs, to spot gaps in the market, to reduce risk, and to inform business decisions.
entries.example: Before opening, a café surveys people nearby about what they would pay and checks how busy rival cafés are.

entries.definition: New information collected first-hand for a particular purpose: surveys, questionnaires, focus groups, observation. Up to date and specific, but slow and costly.
entries.example: A focus group of eight teenagers trying a new drink before launch.

entries.definition: Information that already exists, collected by someone else: internet sources, market reports, government statistics. Quick and cheap, but may be out of date or not specific enough.
entries.example: Using official population figures to estimate how many families live within a mile of a new nursery.

entries.definition: Quantitative data is numbers, which can be counted and compared; qualitative data is opinions and reasons, which explain why. Good research uses both, and the reliability of either depends on how many people were asked and how they were chosen.
entries.example: '62% would buy it' is quantitative; 'they liked the taste but thought it was too sweet' is qualitative.

entries.definition: Splitting a market into groups of customers with similar needs, by location, demographics (age, gender), lifestyle and income, so a business can target each group differently.
entries.example: A gym offering student off-peak passes and a family membership is treating two segments differently.

entries.definition: A diagram that positions competing products on two features, such as price and quality, to show where rivals sit and where there is a gap.
entries.example: If every rival is high price and high quality, the empty low-price corner may be an opportunity — or a sign nobody can make money there.

entries.definition: Other businesses selling to the same customers. Businesses compare themselves on price, quality, location, product range and customer service, and the strength of competition shapes what a new business must do to win customers.
entries.example: A new pizza place next to two established ones needs a clear reason to choose it: faster delivery, a better deal, or something the others don't sell.

entries.definition: Growth a business achieves by **expanding itself**, through new products or by reaching new markets. Also called **organic growth**. It is slower than buying a rival, but the business keeps control and all the profit.
entries.example: A bike maker adds an electric model and launches a website shipping nationwide, taking revenue from £4.2m to £5.46m without buying any other business.

entries.definition: Growth achieved by **joining with another business**, through a merger or a takeover. Also called **inorganic growth**. It is fast, because market share is bought rather than built, but expensive and hard to control.
entries.example: A supermarket chain buys 60% of the shares in a smaller chain, gaining its customers, staff and stores in one move.

entries.definition: Two businesses **agreeing** to join together and become one new business. Both sides want it, which is what separates a merger from a takeover.
entries.example: Two regional bus companies agree to merge, so the new company runs both networks and the two sets of owners share it.

entries.definition: One business buying a **controlling interest** in another, meaning more than half of its shares. It can be agreed, or **hostile** if the business being bought does not want it.
entries.example: Buying 60% of a rival's shares is a takeover; the buyer now owns the rival and can decide how it is run.

entries.definition: A company whose **shares can be bought by anyone** on the stock market. Edexcel names it as the ownership type for growing businesses. It can raise large sums, but the original owners lose control and the accounts become public.
entries.example: A manufacturer becomes a plc and floats 2,000,000 shares at £1.75, raising £3,500,000 that it does not have to repay.

entries.definition: A public limited company selling its shares to the general public for the first time. The money raised is **shares × price per share**, and none of it has to be repaid, but anyone can then buy into the business.
entries.example: 2,000,000 shares at £1.75 raises £3,500,000. No interest is payable, unlike a loan, but the founders no longer own all of the company.

entries.definition: Profit the business **keeps**, after tax has been paid and after dividends have gone to the owners. It is an **internal** source of finance: it costs no interest and gives nothing away, but there is only as much of it as the business has earned.
entries.example: £600,000 profit after tax less £250,000 of dividends leaves £350,000 of retained profit to put towards growth.

entries.definition: Turning something the business **owns but no longer needs**, such as an old building or machinery, into cash. The second **internal** source of finance. Nothing is borrowed, but the asset is gone and may be wanted later.
entries.example: A manufacturer sells an unused unit for £480,000, which with £350,000 of retained profit gives £830,000 towards a £2,000,000 factory.

entries.definition: Money **borrowed** to finance growth, repaid with interest. An **external** source. The owners keep every share, but the repayments are due whether or not the growth works.
entries.example: £900,000 borrowed at 7% costs £63,000 a year in interest, payable even in a year when the new factory stands half empty.

entries.definition: The way national economies have become linked into **one world market**, so a business competes with, buys from and sells to businesses anywhere. Edexcel names four effects: imports, exports, changing business locations and multinationals.
entries.example: A Sheffield bike maker buys frames from Taiwan, sells to Germany through its website, and competes on price with a factory in Shenzhen.

entries.definition: A **tax on imports**, charged by the country the goods arrive in. It makes the imported product dearer, so home-produced goods look cheaper by comparison, which is the point of it.
entries.example: A 12% tariff on a £900 bike adds £108, taking the landed cost to £1,008 before the retailer's own margin. A locally made bike pays nothing.

entries.definition: A group of countries that have agreed to trade **freely with each other**, usually with no tariffs inside the group and a common tariff on goods arriving from outside. A business inside trades freely; one outside pays to get in.
entries.example: A British exporter selling into a trade bloc pays its common external tariff, while a manufacturer inside the bloc sells across it with no tariff at all.

entries.definition: A business with operations in **more than one country**. Because it can choose where to produce and where to book its profit, it can move either to wherever suits it best.
entries.example: A clothing company designs in London, manufactures in Bangladesh and sells across Europe, moving production whenever costs change.

entries.definition: Goods or services a business **sells to overseas markets**. Exporting multiplies the customers available, but brings tariffs, different rules and the cost of changing the marketing mix for each country.
entries.example: A bike maker starts selling to Germany and France through its own website, reaching customers without opening premises in either country.

entries.definition: Spending on **designing and testing new products**. Edexcel names it, alongside **innovation**, as one of the two ways a business reaches **new products**, which is in turn one of the two routes to internal growth, the other being new markets.
entries.example: Two years of research and development produce a lighter frame that no competitor sells, which the business then owns outright.

entries.definition: Bringing something **new to market**: a product, or a new way of making or selling one. Edexcel names it beside research and development as a way of achieving **new products**, which is one of the two routes to internal growth.
entries.example: A bike maker adds an electric model no rival offers, reaching new customers without buying another business.

entries.definition: Meeting today's needs **without stopping future generations meeting theirs**. For a business it is a trade-off: the greener choice usually costs more now, and the benefit is long term.
entries.example: Recyclable packaging costs more per unit than plastic, so profit falls this year in exchange for a business that customers still want to buy from in ten years.
